newsitem.title: USA: Household Int'l buying Transamerica unit for $1.1 billion.
newsitem.headline: Household Int'l buying Transamerica unit for $1.1 billion.

text.p: Household International Inc. said Wednesday it agreed to buy Transamerica Corp.'s consumer finance business for $1.1 billion in cash, a deal that will expand Household's network of offices under the HFC brand.

The HFC consumer finance business is the oldest in the country. Household International also issues private-label and general purpose credit cards in the United States, including the GM Card and the AFL-CIO Union Privilege card.

"There is a certain type of consumer who doesn't like banks. Household International just acquired thousands of relationships with non-bank customers," Piper Jaffray analyst Jeff Evanson said. "That's the core customer that they want."
San Francisco-based Transamerica, which provides financial and life insurance products and services worldwide, had indicated it wanted to sell its consumer finance business, analysts said.
In March, Transamerica said its strategy was to convert its consumer lending operations from branches to a more centralized system.
Duff & Phelps fixed income analyst Chris Reed said the $1.1 billion price reflected "a healthy premium" paid by Household for the Transamerica business.
"They definitely paid a healthy premium for what they acquired as reflected by the purchase price," Reed said. "There was extensive competition for the acquisition."
Transamerica said the consumer finance business had a book value of $487 million as of March 31.
Transamerica said it will use proceeds from the sale to pay off debt and buy back up to 6 million common shares, or about 9 percent of its stock.
Transamerica said it would record a gain on the sale when the deal closes. The sale is subject to regulatory approvals.
Household said it expects the Transaction deal to add slightly to 1997 earnings and contribute about 15 cents to 20 cents a share in 1998. In 1996, the company earned $121 million or $1.77 a share.
"That's the guidance we're giving," a Household spokesman said.
Household, based in Prospect Heights, Ill., said it will finance the deal with a combination of debt and new common equity.
The deal will boost Household's portfolio of core real estate-secured receivables by $3 billion, or almost 38 percent, and will bring its total managed assets to over $50 billion.
The purchase excludes delinquent receivables, it added.
"This acquisition brings us a very high-quality portfolio of real estate-secured loans, a great branch network, and many talented employees," said William Aldinger, chairman of Household.
Household stock rose 75 cents to $92.625 while Transamerica fell 12.5 cents to $87.125, both on the New York Stock Exchange.
